Hey Product Hunt,

Most of us give our coding agent the same few jobs every week. Review this branch. Write the release notes. Find the tests I missed. Each time we paste the same instructions and pick the same permissions again.

GitBot saves that job as a bot. You write the instructions, pick Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, and choose what it's allowed to touch. Then you run it in any repo. Every run gets its own thread, so you can close the tab and come back later.

Bots are easy to share. Last week we ran a 90-minute online build night. Two developers who had never used [...] GitBot built bots and got them into the Library before it ended:

ShipGuard (by Somesh) reviews your branch and ends with merge or block. It cites file and line, and edits nothing.

Sheet Consolidator (by Guru) merges spreadsheet tabs into one table. Nothing to do with code, which we loved.

Try it:

`npm install -g @gitbot-hq/gitbot`
`gitbot start`

It runs on your machine with the agent logins you already have.   
No GitBot account, no hosted database, no telemetry. It's open source.

Coming next: schedules and triggers, so a bot can run without you starting it.

One honest note: GitBot has no network login yet. Keep it on a trusted network and don't expose its port to the internet.

What job do you keep giving your agent that should be a bot? [...] Completed improvements will appear here.

results.content:
Go drop some feature requests

 •

  GitBot — Build bots on the coding agent you already use

  GitBot saves the job you keep retyping into your coding agent as a bot, so you write the instructions once, pick Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, set which folders and commands it may touch, then run it in any repo, with every run opening as its own thread. Bots move between people. You install ones other developers published to the Library, or share yours with a code, and ShipGuard reads a branch and answers merge or block with the file and line cited, editing nothing. Sunny flags that there is no network login yet, so keep the port off the open internet. It runs locally on the agent logins you already have, no account, no telemetry.
 •

  CoIsland — Your whole engineering stack, in a notch [...] CoIsland — Your whole engineering stack, in a notch

  CoIsland watches CI, deploys, errors, incidents and databases across 35 connectors and shows you nothing at all until one of them breaks, at which point it appears in a small island on the edge of your Mac screen. Monitors are plain files, so a database check is the SQL itself, versioned in git with the rest of your code and with no query language to learn first. One click hands an alert to Claude Code, Codex or Cortex Code, and the agent investigates but never resolves it, which stays with you. Elyes built it for his own on-call, and it runs entirely on your Mac with no server in between and no account, at $5.99 once until October 25.
